Well, doctor, it's... it's just this exhaustion. I mean, I don't know if exhaustion is even the right word for it anymore. It's more like this heavy, pulling weight that just drags me down all day, every day. What brought me in is I’m so worn out that even walking from the bedroom to the kitchen feels like hauling lumber all day. And I know what hauling lumber feels like, I used to do some construction work back in my twenties when I was taking a few college classes, and let me tell you, this is worse. I can lie in bed for twelve, fourteen hours, just staring at the ceiling, or maybe dozing off and on, but when I finally force myself to swing my legs over the edge of the mattress, it's like I haven't slept in a week. It takes me twenty minutes just to convince myself to stand up, and by the time I make it to the kitchen to pour a glass of water, I'm ready to collapse again. It's just... it's completely draining the life out of me, and I don't know how much longer I can keep trying to push through it when there's nothing left in the tank to push with.

Well... no, they don't... they don't give me orders, if that's what you mean. They aren't saying, you know, 'go out to the garage and do this' or 'go grab that.' It's not like a set of instructions. Well... that's a good question, doctor, and I've thought about that a lot. I really have. Because when you start hearing things, you start trying to figure out why, you know? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well... I suppose the thoughts really started creeping in around the same time the heavy feeling took over everything. It wasn't an overnight thing, you know? It didn't just hit me all at once. It was more like... like a slow leak in a tire. At first, you just feel a little flat, a little tired. But then, as the weeks went by and I found myself just stuck in that recliner, unable to even muster the energy to go out to the garage and look at my tools... that's when the thoughts started. 

It began as just this vague idea, like, 'maybe it wouldn't be so bad if I just didn't wake up tomorrow.' Just a passing thought. But as I got worse, as I stopped going to work and my wife had to start picking up all those extra shifts, the thought just grew. It got louder, much like those voices in the hallway. And now... now it's just this constant, heavy presence. The thought keeps coming that I should just be dead. It’s like a drumbeat in the background of my mind, just repeating over and over that it would be the easiest solution for everyone.

And the thing is, doctor... it really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because it's one thing to have a passing thought, but it's another thing entirely when you're sitting in that silent house, listening to the refrigerator hum, and you realize you're actually entertaining the idea. When I’m alone, especially when my wife is at work and it's just me and that suffocating quiet... it scares me because I start thinking I might actually do something to make that happen. I start looking around the room, and my mind just goes to these dark, terrible places. I don't want to leave my family, I really don't, but when you're drowning and the voices are telling you you're a burden... sometimes you just want the water to finally take you under. So, it's been building for a while, but it's only recently that it's gotten to the point where I'm genuinely afraid of being left alone with my own mind.

The idea of buying the meat, cleaning the grates, standing out there... it's just too much. I can't make myself care. I can't make myself care about any of it anymore, doctor. It's all just... empty.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any thoughts about death, or wishing you weren't alive, since this heavy feeling started?\n\nPatient: Well... I mean, yes. Yes, I have. It just keeps coming back, over and over. It’s like a broken record playing in the back of my mind all day long. Just this heavy, constant drumbeat of, 'You should be dead. When she's at work and it's just me, the silence gets so heavy, but then... then it's not silent anymore. \n\nI hear voices.
